value.text: This document summarizes the key provisions of The United States Constitution regarding its legislative structure, powers, and admission requirements. Main Points: • Legislative Structure (Pages 1–2): Establishes a bicameral legislature with a Senate (100 senators, elected every six years) and House of Representatives (435 representatives, serving two years). Both houses must meet to conduct business but may adjourn up to three days without consent from the other. All legislative powers are vested in Congress [2]. • Revenue Bills & Eligibility (Pages 1–2): All bills raising revenue must originate in the House of Representatives before reaching the Senate. The document outlines specific eligibility requirements for members, including age and residency [2]. • Legislative Process & Powers (Pages 3–4): Bills require a two-thirds vote to pass both houses and become law; they cannot be rejected by the President without reconsideration. Congress has powers over commerce, currency, money, post offices, and raising armies, while restricting military funding to a two-year term [2]. • State Restrictions & Military (Pages 3–4): States are prohibited from issuing their own currency or entering treaties; they must pay all taxes into the federal treasury. The President serves as Commander-in-Chief of the armed forces [2]. • Judicial Power (Page 5–6): Judicial power is vested in a supreme court and inferior courts, with specific jurisdiction over ambassadors and states versus appellate cases. No state may levy duties on imports or exports without Congress's consent [3]. • Treaty & Admission (Pages 7–9): Treaties made under U.S. authority are the supreme law of the land. New states must receive consent from existing state legislatures and Congress before admission into the Union [4]. • Constitutionality & Oaths (Page 8–9): No person can be convicted of treason without evidence from two witnesses or an open confession; treaties are supreme law, and all federal officers must swear oaths supporting the Constitution [4]. *   **Legislative Structure (Pages 1–2):** Establishes a bicameral legislature with a Senate (100 senators, elected every six years) and House of Representatives (435 representatives, serving two years). Both houses must meet to conduct business but may adjourn up to three days without consent from the other. All legislative powers are vested in Congress [2].
*   **Revenue Bills & Eligibility (Pages 1–2):** All bills raising revenue must originate in the House of Representatives before reaching the Senate. The document outlines specific eligibility requirements for members, including age and residency [2].
*   **Legislative Process & Powers (Pages 3–4):** Bills require a two-thirds vote to pass both houses and become law; they cannot be rejected by the President without reconsideration. Congress has powers over commerce, currency, money, post offices, and raising armies, while restricting military funding to a two-year term [2].
*   **State Restrictions & Military (Pages 3–4):** States are prohibited from issuing their own currency or entering treaties; they must pay all taxes into the federal treasury. The President serves as Commander-in-Chief of the armed forces [2].
*   **Judicial Power (Page 5–6):** Judicial power is vested in a supreme court and inferior courts, with specific jurisdiction over ambassadors and states versus appellate cases. No state may levy duties on imports or exports without Congress's consent [3].
*   **Treaty & Admission (Pages 7–9):** Treaties made under U.S. authority are the supreme law of the land. New states must receive consent from existing state legislatures and Congress before admission into the Union [4].
*   **Constitutionality & Oaths (Page 8–9):** No person can be convicted of treason without evidence from two witnesses or an open confession; treaties are supreme law, and all federal officers must swear oaths supporting the Constitution [4].
